faq.q: Why do the wires in a toaster glow red?
faq.a: They are made of nichrome, an alloy with high electrical resistance. Current passing through it turns into heat, making the wires so hot that they glow red.
asks: What is the heating element in a toaster?

faq.q: How does a toaster keep the bread down?
faq.a: In many toasters an electromagnet holds the lever down while the toaster is on. Older ones use a mechanical catch.
asks: Why does the lever stay down?

faq.q: How does a toaster know when to pop up?
faq.a: It does not see the toast. A timer, either a small electronic circuit or a bending bimetal strip in older toasters, releases the latch after the time set on the dial.
asks: What does the toaster dial do?

faq.a: Heat makes sugars and proteins on the surface of the bread react together, called the Maillard reaction. It creates brown colours and toasty flavours.

faq.q: Why should you never put a fork in a toaster?
faq.a: The bare wires are live with mains electricity, so touching them with metal could give a deadly shock. Unplug the toaster before freeing stuck bread.
asks: Is it dangerous to get toast out with a knife?

facts: Toaster heating wires are usually nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists electricity and does not oxidise easily.
Charles Strite filed a patent for an automatic pop-up toaster in 1919.
